# Requirements traceability

**Generated by `tools/make_traceability.py`. Do not edit by hand.**

Measured at `8194ca4`. Total tests collected: **833**.

Read each row left to right: somebody asked for this → it became a
story → here is the code → here is what proves it. A row that cannot
be completed is work that was never really finished.

This is generated because a hand-typed traceability table makes its
promise once and then quietly stops being true — which is worse than
not having one, because it still looks like evidence.

**Read the last column precisely.** A file is listed when it
*imports* the module — a real join, read from the AST, not a word
match. The number beside it is how many tests **that file** holds,
not how many are about this feature: `test_device_scoping.py` imports
three checks and is counted under all three. It is an upper bound on
the evidence, and saying so is cheaper than pretending otherwise.

**The last column and the total above it count different things,**
deliberately, and the column now says which so nobody has to work
it out by subtraction. The column counts `def test_` FUNCTIONS in
the file; the total counts what pytest actually COLLECTS, and
collection expands each parametrised function into one case per
parameter. So a file holding parametrised tests contributes more to
the total than its own column shows. Neither number is wrong, but
adding the column up will not reach the total, and a reader who
tries deserves to be told why rather than concluding the table is
broken. No worked example is given here on purpose: it would be a
hand-written number inside a generated file, which is the failure
this document exists to avoid.

## The three feature shapes, read from the registries themselves

| Shape | Registered in | Features |
|---|---|---|
| Producer `run(bf)` | `CHECKS` | `access_control`, `policy_compliance`, `routing` |
| Post-processor `refine(results)` | `POST_PROCESSORS` | `risk` |
| Separate entry point | *neither* | `change_impact` |

`change_impact` is in **neither** registry on purpose: it needs two
snapshots, so it cannot satisfy `run(bf)`. See
`docs/design/pipeline-feature-shapes.md`, adopted by all four.

These are committed on purpose and are the single exception to the
no-configs-in-git rule: we invented them, so they describe nobody's
real network.

## What this table does NOT prove

That a test is a **good** test. A path from a requirement to
something executable is a weaker claim than "this is verified", and
conflating the two is the failure this project keeps finding.

Test quality is checked elsewhere: `tests/test_suite_hygiene.py`
asserts every test file can fail, and every non-trivial safety guard
is mutation-tested — deliberately broken, with the suite confirmed to
die — under both Batfish states.
